title: B-T-Ch

segments.voice: Yesterday, N-D-R: neder, a vow. Your line was vow. Was there one you kept, even a small one? Today, the root that sits underneath any promise someone else makes to you. Day one thousand four hundred twelve.

A man in the Talmud goes by Nachum Ish Gamzu, and his nickname is a sentence. Whatever happened to him, he would say gam zu l'tovah: this too is for the good. Once, the story goes, he was sent to the emperor with a chest of jewels as a gift. On the way he stopped at an inn, and in the night the chest was emptied and filled with dirt. He arrived, opened it before the emperor, and there was only earth. The Talmud tells how the dirt turned out to be useful after all, and he came home honored. Whatever you make of the ending, the man had a habit. Today's root is the name for it.
screen: `NACHUM ISH GAMZU.` → `A CHEST OF JEWELS, FULL OF DIRT.` → `THIS TOO IS FOR THE GOOD.`

segments.voice: B-T-Ch. Bet, tet, chet. Bitachon: trust. Turn it a few ways. First, the verb. Proverbs puts it plainly: "Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding." Trust there is something you do, and the verse sets it against leaning on your own reading of events. Second, the same letters mean safety. In Leviticus the people are promised that if they keep the commandments, "ye shall dwell in the land in safety." The Hebrew there is la-vetach, from this root. And a psalm uses it at bedtime: "I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety." In this root, trusting and being safe live under one roof. Trust is somewhere you can lie down. Third, a book. The Jewish philosopher Bachya ibn Pakuda wrote Duties of the Heart, and one of its gates is the gate of trust. He treats trust as work done inside, by the heart, while a person still does their part in the world. Fourth, back to Nachum. Jewish thinkers have argued about what bitachon expects. Some teach that trust means confidence that things will turn out well. Others teach that it means confidence that whatever comes is held by God, even when it doesn't look good. Nachum's sentence can be heard either way. What both readings share is the moment he said it: with the dirt in front of him, before he knew how the story would end.
screen: `TRUST, AND LEAN NOT.` · `THE SAME LETTERS MEAN SAFETY.` · `BACHYA'S GATE OF TRUST.` · `SAID BEFORE THE ENDING.` · then, large: `TRUST IS SOMEWHERE TO LIE DOWN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: trust someone with one thing. Settle, and breathe. Let your shoulders drop, the way they would if you were lying down in that psalm. Now find one thing you've been carrying alone: a task, a worry, a question you haven't asked. Then think of one person who could hold part of it. A friend, a sibling, a coworker. Don't script the conversation. Just see yourself handing it over, and notice what your hands feel like after. If you pray, you can say the psalm's line: I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep. The bell holds the time.
screen: `ONE THING YOU CARRY ALONE.` · `ONE PERSON WHO COULD HOLD IT.` · `HAND IT OVER.`

segments.voice: B-T-Ch. Bet, tet, chet: the root of bitachon, trust, and of betach, safety. Nachum's habit. Today's word.
Your line: trust. Today, hand one real thing to one real person, and let them do it their way. Day one thousand four hundred twelve.

howItsDone: Jewish teaching on bitachon, trust in God, runs from Proverbs and the Psalms to the gate of trust in Bachya ibn Pakuda's Duties of the Heart; some Jews repeat Nachum Ish Gamzu's words, gam zu l'tovah, this too is for the good.

original.note: Hebrew: trust, from bet, tet, chet, the same root as betach, safety.

trapdoor: what you thought: trust means expecting everything to go well.
what it means: bitachon is leaning on God, and the same root gives betach, safety, a place to lie down.

notes: Taanit 21a paraphrased: Nachum Ish Gamzu sent to the emperor with a chest of precious stones; at an inn the contents were replaced with earth; the earth proved miraculous (in the Talmud, Elijah suggests it is Abraham's earth), and he was sent home honored. The hook keeps the ending vague ('turned out to be useful'). Confirm.
Leviticus 25:18 la-vetach and Psalm 4:9 la-vetach: both from the root bet-tet-chet. Confirm.
Bachya ibn Pakuda's Gate of Trust: summarized as trust being inner work while a person still makes effort in the world (hishtadlut). Confirm this summary is fair.
Two views of bitachon given without ranking (confidence in a good outcome vs. confidence that whatever happens is from God). Confirm both are fairly described; no names attached deliberately.
Quotations from KJV rather than JPS 1917 because the KJV wording is certain; confirm or swap for JPS 1917.
